cards.title: A LangGraph node is usually just a LangChain chain with a name.
cards.body: Inside a node you write ordinary LangChain: `prompt | llm | parser`, or `create_agent(...)`. LangGraph never replaces that code; it decides *when* it runs, *what state it reads*, and *whether it runs again*. Think of a chain as a function body and the graph as the call graph around it.
cards.why: Interviewers ask 'LangChain or LangGraph?' expecting 'both, at different layers'. Chains do work; the graph schedules work.

cards.title: Spot the rung from the symptom, not the framework name.
cards.body: Each rung changes one thing: who decides the next step. Chain: you, at write time. Agent: the model, per step, picking tools. Multi-agent: an agent picking another agent. The same bug report sounds different on each rung.

quiz.question: A teammate says: 'The billing specialist keeps handing the ticket back to the triage agent, and triage sends it straight back — infinite ping-pong.' Which rung is this system on, and what is the fix family?
options: Chain — add a retry decorator
Agent — lower the tool count
Multi-agent — add a handoff budget or a terminal 'escalate' route
Chain — swap to a bigger model
quiz.explain: Agents routing to agents is the multi-agent rung, and the classic failure there is a routing loop. Fixes live in control flow: cap handoffs per thread, add a terminal escalation node, or let the supervisor remember who already touched the ticket. Model size and retries do not change who decides next.

cards.title: The ReAct loop exits on the first `AIMessage` with no `tool_calls`.
cards.body: There is no 'done' tool. After every model turn the agent checks `response.tool_calls`: non-empty means run them and loop; empty means the model chose to answer, so return. That is the whole termination rule behind `create_agent`.
cards.why: Debug tip: an agent that 'never finishes' is a model that keeps emitting tool calls. Log `len(msg.tool_calls)` per turn and the loop becomes visible.

cards.title: `.assign()` adds a key to the dict flowing through a chain — nothing is lost.
cards.body: `RunnablePassthrough.assign(ctx=retriever)` keeps the original input keys and adds `ctx`. The plain dict-in-a-chain form *replaces* the input with the dict you wrote. Use `assign` when later steps still need the question.
cards.why: Most 'KeyError: question' bugs in RAG chains are a dict step that swallowed the input.

code.src:
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough
from operator import itemgetter

chain = (
    RunnablePassthrough.assign(ctx=itemgetter("q") | retriever)
    | prompt                      # sees both "q" and "ctx"
    | llm
)
chain.invoke({"q": "What is RRF?"})

cards.title: A handoff is a tool that returns `Command(goto=..., graph=Command.PARENT)`.
cards.body: Workers hand off by calling a tool whose return value is a `Command`. `graph=Command.PARENT` tells LangGraph the jump targets a node in the *parent* graph, not inside the worker's own subgraph. The supervisor becomes optional: routing lives in the tools.
cards.why: This is the 'swarm' shape. Know both shapes and when the decision should sit in a central router versus with the worker.

cards.title: A reducer is a tiny merge function that sits on one state key.
cards.body: Two parallel nodes write `{"hits": [...]}`. Without a reducer the second write is a conflict. With `Annotated[list, operator.add]` the writes queue up and the reducer folds them into the channel, in superstep order. The reducer never sees the whole state — only the old value and one new value.

diagram.caption: One key, one reducer, any number of writers.

cards.title: `stream_mode="custom"` streams *your* events — progress, not tokens.
cards.body: Call `get_stream_writer()` inside a node and whatever you pass to it arrives in the consumer under the `custom` mode. Use it for 'fetched 3/10 pages' style progress that is neither a token nor a state update.
cards.why: Product UIs need progress for long tool calls. This avoids abusing `messages` or polluting state with UI chatter.

cards.title: BM25 wins on tokens the embedding model never learned.
cards.body: Dense retrieval maps meaning; it is weak on strings with no meaning — SKUs, error codes, ticket IDs, function names. Lexical search matches them exactly. Hybrid search exists because every corpus has both kinds of queries.

quiz.question: Users search an internal runbook for `ERR_CONN_RESET_4091`. Pure vector search returns generic networking docs. Which single change most directly fixes this?
options: Increase top-k from 5 to 20
Add a BM25 retriever and fuse with RRF
Switch to a larger embedding model
Lower chunk_size to 200
quiz.explain: The query is an exact token with no semantic neighbourhood; only lexical matching finds it reliably. A bigger embedding model still has not seen that string, and more top-k just adds more generic docs. RRF lets the BM25 hit surface without comparing incomparable scores.

cards.title: Span *type* is what makes the MLflow UI render retrieved docs as docs.
cards.body: `@mlflow.trace(span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER)` plus a list-of-Document output gets a special panel with chunk text, scores and sources. The same function tagged as a generic span shows raw JSON. Types also feed the RAG evaluators that look for retriever spans.

quiz.question: Your retriever is traced but MLflow's RAG scorers report 'no retrieval context found' and the UI shows raw JSON. Most likely cause?
options: The LLM span is missing
The retriever span has the default span_type, not RETRIEVER
Autologging is disabled
The trace has no session_id tag
quiz.explain: Scorers and the UI locate context by span type. Set `span_type=SpanType.RETRIEVER` (and return Documents or dicts with page_content) and both start working. Autolog is clearly on — the span exists — and session tags affect grouping, not retrieval rendering.

cards.title: Scrub PII where the data *crosses a boundary*, not where it is born.
cards.body: Three boundaries: user → agent (input), agent → tool (arguments), agent → user (output). A guardrail is cheap at a boundary and expensive inside a prompt. Pick the boundary the data actually crosses.

quiz.question: Your agent may call a third-party `send_sms(to, text)` tool. Legal says no customer email address may ever reach that vendor. Where does the check belong?
options: In the system prompt: 'never include emails'
At the tool-call boundary: validate/scrub `text` before `send_sms` executes
In the output guardrail that checks the final reply
In the retriever
quiz.explain: The vendor sees tool *arguments*, so the only boundary that matters is agent → tool. A middleware or tool wrapper that inspects args before execution is deterministic; a prompt rule is advisory and the output guardrail runs too late — the SMS has already gone.

cards.title: `create_agent(..., response_format=Model)` gives you `result["structured_response"]`.
cards.body: You do not need a separate `with_structured_output` call at the end of an agent. Pass a Pydantic model as `response_format` and the final answer is produced as that type, available next to the messages.
cards.why: Interview-grade detail: the tool-calling loop and the final typed answer are two different model behaviours; `response_format` wires the second onto the first.

code.src:
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain.agents import create_agent

class Triage(BaseModel):
    team: str
    priority: int

agent = create_agent(model, tools=[lookup], response_format=Triage)
out = agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Card declined twice")]})
print(out["structured_response"].team, out["structured_response"].priority)

cards.title: The deep agent's to-do list is a *context-engineering* device, not project management.
cards.body: `write_todos` makes the agent restate its plan every few steps. The value is not the list; it is that the plan keeps re-entering the context window near the end, where attention is strongest, so a 60-step run does not drift from step 3's intent.
cards.why: Same trick as a human rereading their notes mid-task. When you see an agent lose the plot after 20 tool calls, this is the missing piece.

cards.title: Managed or self-hosted deep agent? Decide by *who owns the loop*.
cards.body: A managed deep agent is a definition — prompt, tools, sub-agents, files — that LangSmith compiles, schedules and traces for you. A self-hosted LangGraph graph is code you run. Pick managed when the control flow is the standard deep-agent loop; pick a graph when you need custom edges.

quiz.question: Your team needs a research agent with three sub-agents and a filesystem, no custom routing, and wants it deployed and traced today with no servers. Which fits?
options: Hand-write a StateGraph and deploy to Agent Server
Managed Deep Agent via `define_deep_agent()`
A LangChain chain with a very long prompt
A cron on the Agent Server
quiz.explain: The requirement *is* the standard deep-agent loop, so the managed path removes all infra. The moment you need a non-standard edge — say, a compliance check between planner and workers — you drop to a StateGraph. The chain and cron options do not provide sub-agents at all.

cards.title: For an auditor, a policy is a claim; a trace query is evidence.
cards.body: ISO 42001 asks for an AI management system you can *show*. In practice that is four queries: which agent (agent record), what it did (traces with inputs/outputs or their hashed shape), who approved risky actions (HITL interrupts + feedback), and what would have alerted you (online evaluator rules). Write the queries before the audit, not during.
cards.why: Compliance work is cheap if your observability already has stable identifiers. It is impossible if traces are anonymous blobs.

cards.title: Everything hangs off the agent record: environments, deployments, traces, outcomes.
cards.body: The record is the stable identity (owner, immutable ID, type). Environments (dev/staging/prod) belong to it; deployments belong to environments; traces and outcomes point back up the chain. Rename a deployment and nothing breaks, because the ID lives on the record.

diagram.caption: Cost per outcome rolls up to the record.

cards.title: `langgraph deploy list --json | jq '.[].url'` — the URL is now in the JSON.
cards.body: langgraph-cli 0.4.44 added `url` to the JSON listing and let you target a BYOC data plane with only an API key. Together they make a deploy-then-smoke-test step scriptable in CI without the UI.
cards.why: A deploy that cannot print its own URL cannot be smoke-tested automatically. This closes that gap.

code.src:
export LANGSMITH_API_KEY=...
langgraph deploy --config langgraph.json
URL=$(langgraph deploy list --json | jq -r '.[0].url')
curl -s "$URL/ok"           # health check
curl -s "$URL/assistants/search" -X POST -d '{}' \
     -H "x-api-key: $LANGSMITH_API_KEY" | jq length

cards.title: Bring your own `httpx` client to `ChatAnthropic` — proxies, mTLS and pool limits in one place.
cards.body: langchain-anthropic 1.7.13 accepts caller-supplied HTTP and SDK clients. Build one `httpx.Client` with your corporate proxy, CA bundle and connection limits, and hand it in; the model class stops creating its own.
cards.why: Follows last week's lesson: a pool belongs to a client. Now you can own that client instead of fighting the default one.

code.src:
import httpx
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic

http = httpx.Client(
    proxy="http://proxy.corp:8080",
    verify="/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem",
    limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=20),
    timeout=60,
)
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-5", http_client=http)

cards.title: MLflow 3.18's Issues tab clusters failing traces so you stop reading them one by one.
cards.body: Point it at an experiment and it groups recurring failure patterns — wrong tool, refusal, timeout — into issues linked back to example traces. Run it on demand or on a daily schedule. Needs a SQL-backed tracking server, not file-based.
cards.why: This is the MLflow answer to LangSmith Engine's 'issues' step: traces in, a ranked list of what is actually going wrong out.

cards.title: A skill registry versions agent *instructions* the way a model registry versions weights.
cards.body: MLflow 3.18 ships an experimental Skill Registry: register a skill folder from local disk, Git, OCI or ZIP, then pin it by version or by alias such as `production`. Agents resolve the alias at start-up, so promoting a skill is a pointer move, not a redeploy.
cards.why: Prompts, skills and models are all artefacts that change independently. Each needs its own alias-based promotion path.

cards.title: `interrupt_mode="per_call"` asks once *per tool call*, not once per turn.
cards.body: Default HITL batching pauses once with all pending tool calls in one interrupt. `per_call` pauses separately for each, so an approval UI can show one action at a time and resume each with its own decision.
cards.why: Batched approval is faster; per-call is safer when one turn mixes a harmless read with a dangerous write.

code.src:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import HumanInTheLoopMiddleware

hitl = HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(
    interrupt_on={"delete_record": True, "send_email": True},
    interrupt_mode="per_call",
)
agent = create_agent(model, tools=tools, middleware=[hitl],
                     checkpointer=checkpointer)

cards.title: To the agent, an MCP tool is just another `@tool` — the adapter does the translation.
cards.body: `MultiServerMCPClient` connects to one or more MCP servers, lists their tools and wraps each as a LangChain tool with the server's JSON schema as the argument schema. The ReAct loop cannot tell the difference. Newer LangChain also exposes this under `langchain.mcp` (beta).
cards.why: MCP is how you stop writing a bespoke wrapper for every SaaS. The trade: you now depend on the *server's* docstrings being good.

cards.title: Since langchain-core 1.7, tool-call arguments stream as `tool-call-delta` events — upgrade the *client* first.
cards.body: Arguments used to arrive only when the tool call was complete. Now fragments stream as they are generated, which is what lets a UI show 'searching for: lang…' live. Consumers on older `langchain-core` or old UI packages drop the deltas, which is why the docs say upgrade clients before servers.
cards.why: Explains last week's `openai-stream-toolcall-args` fix: the streaming contract changed, and a few consumers lagged behind it.

cards.title: Summarisation middleware is a valve before the model call: compress old turns, keep recent ones verbatim.
cards.body: When the running token count crosses a threshold, the middleware replaces older messages with one summary message and leaves the last N turns intact. It runs inside the agent loop, so you never write the 'summarise then wipe' node yourself.

diagram.caption: Below budget: straight to the model. Above: compress first.

cards.title: Final-answer evals grade the destination; trajectory evals grade the route.
cards.body: A trajectory evaluator looks at the *sequence* of tool calls — did it search before answering, did it avoid the forbidden tool, how many steps. Exact-match trajectories are brittle; 'contains these calls in any order' or an LLM judge over the trace is the usual middle ground. LangSmith's trajectory rules now accept trace and tree filters.
cards.why: Two agents can both answer correctly while one made 40 calls and the other 4. Only trajectory metrics see that.

cards.title: LangSmith Sandboxes gained *volumes* (beta) and `cp`/`ls` in the CLI.
cards.body: Volumes are persistent disks you create, list, clone and attach to sandboxes, so an agent's working files outlive one sandbox. `langsmith sandboxes cp` and `ls` move and inspect files, `--preserve-memory-on-stop` keeps RAM state, and `snapshot capture --include-memory` freezes a whole running sandbox.
cards.why: This turns a sandbox from a throwaway shell into a resumable workspace — the piece deep agents needed for multi-day coding tasks.

cards.title: Advanced code evaluators are now on by default — your Python runs in a sandbox next to the trace.
cards.body: No opt-in flag anymore on Cloud. Write a Python function, LangSmith runs it in an isolated sandbox against each sampled trace and writes the result back as feedback. On BYOC and self-hosted the switch is `SANDBOX_FEATURE_ENABLED`; the old `codeEvaluatorV2Enabled` field is ignored.

diagram.caption: Same shape as MLflow online scorers — different host.

cards.title: Breaking: 'teams' are now 'user groups' in LangSmith — headers, tags and permissions all changed.
cards.body: Permissions moved to `organization:user-groups:*` / `workspaces:user-groups:*`, and gateway traces now carry `gateway.user_group_ids`. The `X-LangSmith-Team-Tags` header, `ls_team:` tags, gateway policies matching on `team_id`, and `gateway.team_ids` filters stop working.

quiz.question: After the rename, your cost dashboard that filters gateway traces by `gateway.team_ids` shows zero spend. What happened?
options: The gateway stopped tracing
The field was renamed to `gateway.user_group_ids`; the old filter matches nothing
Your API key lost the `teams:*` permission so traces are hidden
Cost attribution moved to the agent record
quiz.explain: Traces are still written; the attribute key changed. Update the filter and any `team_id` gateway policies in the same pass, and replace `X-LangSmith-Team-Tags` headers in clients. Checking for renamed identifiers is step one of any breaking-change triage.

cards.title: Reported: LangSmith's standard terms change on 1 Dec — check the training opt-out and hide inputs regardless.
cards.body: A policy write-up (24 Nov) reads the new Standard Terms as allowing use of customer data to improve the platform unless you opt out in settings, for self-serve plans; enterprise terms reportedly keep the old no-training commitment. Verify against LangChain's own terms and FAQ. Either way, `LANGSMITH_HIDE_INPUTS` / `LANGSMITH_HIDE_OUTPUTS` or `hide_inputs=` callables keep payloads out of the vendor entirely.
cards.why: Data-residency questions come up in every enterprise agent review. The technical control (scrub before send) does not depend on reading the contract correctly.

cards.title: `reasoning_effort` is now a *standard* chat-model parameter in the LangChain monorepo (Nov 23 release wave).
cards.body: Instead of each provider inventing `thinking={...}` or `reasoning={...}`, you set one field at init and the provider class maps it. The same wave made OpenAI prompt caching explicit and shipped `langchain-ollama` 1.2.0 with thinking levels (needs ollama ≥ 0.6.3).
cards.why: Model routers and fallback middleware need provider-neutral knobs. Effort was the last big one that was not standardised.

code.src:
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

fast = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5-mini", reasoning_effort="low")
deep = init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", reasoning_effort="high")

def pick(difficulty: str):
    return deep if difficulty == "hard" else fast

cards.title: `otel.span.*` metadata: OpenTelemetry attributes now ride into LangSmith as run metadata.
cards.body: When traces arrive through the OTel path, span attributes are copied onto the run under an `otel.span.` prefix, so you can filter LangSmith runs by `otel.span.http.route` or your own attributes. Self-hosted can turn it off with `OTEL_PASSTHROUGH_TO_METADATA_ENABLED=false`.
cards.why: If your platform team already tags OTel spans with tenant and region, you get those filters in LangSmith for free instead of re-tagging in code.
